pos: n. (the common sleeping hall of a monastery, reached from the church by the night stair)
etymology: Latin dormitorium, a sleeping place, from dormire, to sleep; the same root gives dormant.
biblical_def: The dormitory was the common sleeping hall of a religious house, a long upper chamber lined with beds, connected to the choir by a night stair so that the brethren could come down to nocturns without going outside. It is the plainest piece of monastic architecture and the most revealing, because it abolished privacy: a man slept where his brothers could see him, and the rule forbade a lamp to be put out. The arrangement answered a real pastoral concern about secret sin, and the instinct that Christians should be visible to one another has warrant — “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed” (Jam 5:16). But Scripture's treatment of sleep is warmer than a rule and a lamp. Sleep is a gift and a sign of trust: “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” (Psa 4:8), “for so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2), and “thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet” (Pro 3:24). A house that broke its rest into fragments for the night office gained the psalmody and lost something the Psalter itself commends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dormitory as a place, building or room to sleep in, and also a burial place; dormant as sleeping, at rest; and sleep as that state in which the voluntary functions are suspended.
webster_full: DORMITORY, n. A place, building or room to sleep in; also, a place for the burial of the dead; a cemetery.
DORMANT, a. Sleeping; hence, at rest; not in action; as, a dormant passion; dormant claims or titles.
SLEEP, n. That state of an animal in which the voluntary exertion of his mental and corporeal powers is suspended.
REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind; quiet; repose; a state of sleep.
COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; general; public.
scriptures: Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
Pro 3:24
When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.
Jam 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
corruption_summary: The common sleeping hall: privacy abolished to prevent secret sin, in a house whose night office broke the rest Scripture calls a gift.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sleep as a creaturely gift received in trust. “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows” (Psa 127:2) rebukes the sleepless striver, and a monastic timetable that treated rest as a concession to weakness was closer to that striving than it knew.

The live defect is the attempt to secure holiness by architecture. A lamp and an open hall can prevent an act and cannot touch a heart, and Scripture locates the remedy in confession between brothers rather than in surveillance: “Confess your faults one to another” (Jam 5:16). Watchfulness is nonetheless commanded, and the dormitory's own hour supplies the text: “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mar 13:36).
roots_summary: Latin dormire, to sleep; Hebrew shenah (H8142), sleep; Hebrew shakab (H7901), to lie down; Greek koimao (G2837), to fall asleep; Greek gregoreo (G1127), to watch.
roots_lines: Latin dormitorium — a sleeping place; in older English also a burial ground, which is the same metaphor Scripture uses.
Hebrew shenah (H8142) — sleep; “so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2).
Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down; “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep” (Psa 4:8).
Greek koimao (G2837) — to fall asleep, and so to die; the root of cemetery.
Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to be awake, to watch; “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mar 13:36).
usage: “for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” (Psa 4:8) — the ground of a Christian's rest.
“thy sleep shall be sweet” (Pro 3:24) — a promise, not a concession.
“Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead” (Eph 5:14) — the other sleep, which no hall can prevent.

pos: n. (the obedientiary responsible for a monastery's provisions, stores and estates; its chief steward)
etymology: Latin cellarium, a storeroom or pantry, from cella, a chamber; the keeper of the stores.
biblical_def: The cellarer was the chief steward of a monastic house: he bought the grain, ran the granges, paid the servants, kept the stores and fed the community and its guests. In a large abbey he was effectively the chief executive, and Benedict's rule devotes a careful chapter to him, requiring a man who is wise, sober, not greedy and not given to delay, who will not grieve the brethren and who will treat the pots of the house as sacred vessels. That chapter is unusually close to Scripture, because stewardship is a biblical office with a biblical standard. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2) is the whole of it; and the Lord's own portrait of a good administrator is a man who feeds those under him on time: “Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?” (Luk 12:42). Joseph is the pattern — “he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand” (Gen 39:4). The besetting temptation of the office is equally scriptural, and Paul names it when he requires a steward of God to be “not given to filthy lucre” (Tit 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cellarer as a monk who has the care of the cellar, or who has the charge of procuring and keeping the provisions; steward as a man employed to manage the affairs of another; and provision as a stock provided, victuals, food.
webster_full: CELLARER, n. An officer in a monastery who has the care of the cellar, or the charge of procuring and keeping the provisions.
CELLAR, n. A room under a building, used as a repository of liquors, provisions and other stores.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, collect the rents, and keep the accounts.
PROVISION, n. A stock of provided; a store or stock collected; particularly, a stock of food; victuals; as provisions for the army.
FAITHFUL, a. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; true to allegiance; constant in the performance of duties or services.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?
Gen 39:4
And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.
Tit 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
corruption_summary: The monastery's chief steward: a biblical office with a biblical standard, and the office in the house most exposed to filthy lucre.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithfulness as the sole measure of an administrator. “it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2) says nothing about flair or growth, and a church that appoints its managers on any other basis has changed the qualification.

The live corruption is the one Paul attaches to the office by name. A man who handles money for a religious body and answers to no audit will in time answer to his appetite, which is why Scripture pairs the trust with a reckoning: “give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward” (Luk 16:2). The apostles themselves appointed men of honest report to handle a fund rather than handling it alone — “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3).
roots_summary: Latin cellarium, a storeroom; Greek oikonomos (G3623), a house-manager; Greek oikonomia (G3622), stewardship; Hebrew asher al-habbayith, over the house; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful.
roots_lines: Latin cellarium — a pantry or store; the office named from the room it keeps.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a household manager; “that faithful and wise steward” (Luk 12:42).
Greek oikonomia (G3622) — stewardship, administration; “give an account of thy stewardship” (Luk 16:2).
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; “that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).
Hebrew paqid (H6496) — an appointed overseer; Joseph's office in Potiphar's house and in Egypt.
usage: “all that he had he put into his hand” (Gen 39:4) — the trust a cellarer held.
“as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry” (Tit 1:7) — the character required.
“to give them their portion of meat in due season” (Luk 12:42) — the work itself, plainly described.

pos: n. (the obedientiary charged with the church fabric, vessels, vestments, lights and bells; the sacristan)
etymology: Latin sacrista, from sacer, sacred; the keeper of sacred things. English sexton is the same word worn down.
biblical_def: The sacrist kept the church: its fabric, its plate and vestments, its lights, its relics and its bells, and he rang the hours that governed the whole house. In a great abbey the office carried a large income and a building department. The work has an Old Testament precedent in the Levites charged with the vessels and the service of the tabernacle — “I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve, even the service of the tabernacle of the congregation” (Num 18:21) — and the care of holy things is treated there with great seriousness. But the New Testament makes a decisive shift that the office never absorbed. The temple is gone and the sanctuary is people: “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5), and “Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” (1Co 3:16). A man who keeps a building well is doing an honourable thing, and a church that confuses the keeping of its fabric with the keeping of its holiness has mistaken the vessel for the sacrifice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sacrist as a person retained in a cathedral to copy music and take care of the books; sacristan as an officer who has the care of the utensils or movables of a church, a sexton; and sacristy as an apartment in a church where the sacred utensils are kept.
webster_full: SACRIST, n. A person retained in a cathedral to copy out music for the choir, and take care of the books.
SACRISTAN, n. An officer who has the care of the utensils or movables of a church; a sexton.
SACRISTY, n. An apartment in a church where the sacred utensils, vestments and other valuable things are kept.
SEXTON, n. An under officer of the church, whose business is to take care of the vessels, vestments, etc. belonging to the church.
VESSEL, n. Any thing hollow and capable of containing liquor or other substance; also, in scripture, a person.
scriptures: And, behold, I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve, even the service of the tabernacle of the congregation.
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
corruption_summary: The keeper of a church's fabric, plate and bells: an honourable charge, in an office that could mistake the care of a building for the care of holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the drift of expense from people to stone, and Haggai names it: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4) is the rebuke in one direction, while the later prophets rebuke the reverse — a magnificent sanctuary and a neglected poor. The late medieval abbeys often managed both faults at once, with gilded plate in the sacristy and a resentful tenantry outside.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the New Testament location of the temple. “ye are the temple of God” (1Co 3:16) does not make buildings worthless; it makes them instruments, and it settles for ever which of the two a church may not neglect.
roots_summary: Latin sacer, sacred; Hebrew kodesh (H6944), holiness; Hebrew keli (H3627), a vessel; Greek naos (G3485), a temple sanctuary; Greek skeuos (G4632), a vessel.
roots_lines: Latin sacer, sacrista — sacred, and the keeper of sacred things; English sexton is the same word.
Hebrew kodesh (H6944) — holiness, a holy thing; the category the sacrist's charge belonged to.
Hebrew keli (H3627) — a vessel, implement; the tabernacle's furniture, carried by the Levites.
Greek naos (G3485) — the sanctuary itself; “ye are the temple of God” (1Co 3:16).
Greek skeuos (G4632) — a vessel; in Paul a person, chosen or prepared.
usage: “for their service which they serve” (Num 18:21) — the Levitical charge the office imitated.
“built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5) — where the sanctuary now is.
“and this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4) — the prophet's rebuke about a neglected house of God.

pos: n. (the obedientiary in charge of a monastery's infirmary, nursing the sick and aged of the house)
etymology: Latin infirmus, not firm, weak or sick, from in-, not, and firmus, strong; the keeper of the weak.
biblical_def: The infirmarer ran the monastic infirmary: a separate hall with its own chapel and kitchen where the sick, the aged and the dying of the house were nursed, with a relaxed diet and a relaxed rule. Benedict's chapter on the sick is one of the most humane passages in medieval literature and rests on one verse: the care of the sick is to come before and above all else, for in them Christ is served. He had read it straight. “I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36) is the charter, and “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40) is the reason. Scripture adds the elders' prayer — “Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (Jam 5:14) — and the standing rebuke to any shepherd who neglects this work: “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken” (Eze 34:4). The monastic infirmaries are the ancestors of the European hospital, and on this one point the cloister's record is better than most of what replaced it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infirmary as a lodging for the sick, a hospital or place where the sick are lodged and nursed; infirm as not firm or sound, weak, feeble; and nurse as a person who has the care of the sick.
webster_full: INFIRMARY, n. A lodging for the sick; a hospital, or place where the sick and infirm are received and nursed.
INFIRM, a. Not firm or sound; weak; feeble; as an infirm body or constitution.
INFIRMITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness; also, a failing; a fault.
NURSE, n. A person who has the care of the sick, or of the infirm and aged; one who tends and attends another in weakness.
VISIT, v.t. To go to with care and relief, as the sick and afflicted; to attend, as a physician.
scriptures: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Jam 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
Eze 34:4

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
corruption_summary: The monastery's nurse: the cloister's plainest obedience to Christ, and the ancestor of the European hospital.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that nursing the sick is not a profession the church may outsource but an obedience Christ identifies with himself: “ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40). Congregations with no practical ministry to their own sick and aged should read Benedict on this subject and be rebuked by him.

The live defect of the monastic version was its boundary. The infirmary served the house, and only secondarily the village at the gate; the hospital proper had to be invented alongside it. “neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4) judges a care that waits to be approached rather than going to seek.
roots_summary: Latin infirmus, weak; Greek astheneia (G769), weakness or sickness; Greek episkeptomai (G1980), to visit and look after; Hebrew chalah (H2470), to be sick; Greek therapeuo (G2323), to heal or serve.
roots_lines: Latin infirmus — not firm, weak; the office named for those it serves.
Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity, sickness; the New Testament's broad word for it.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit with care, to look after; “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36).
Greek therapeuo (G2323) — to serve and so to heal; the root of therapy.
Hebrew chalah (H2470) — to be sick, weak; “thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness” (Psa 41:3).
usage: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36) — the charter of every Christian infirmary.
“let him call for the elders of the church” (Jam 5:14) — the congregational duty alongside the nursing.
“neither have ye healed that which was sick” (Eze 34:4) — the charge against a shepherd who omits it.

pos: n. (the superior of a priory of nuns, or the second in rank under an abbess)
etymology: Latin prior, former or superior, with the English feminine suffix -ess; the first among the sisters.
biblical_def: A prioress is the head of a priory of women, or in a great abbey the deputy under the abbess. She ruled a household: she admitted and professed novices, held the house's chapter, disciplined, administered estates and answered to a visiting bishop. English priories of nuns were mostly small and poor, and the office was often a hard one carried with little money and much interference. Scripture gives real and honourable authority to women within its own order — a wife “guide the house” (1Ti 5:14), the woman of Proverbs runs an estate, buys a field and directs servants — and it gives older women a teaching charge over younger: “that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things” (Tit 2:3). A prioress exercising oversight over a household of women is therefore doing something Scripture recognises, not something it forbids. What Scripture withholds from her — and what the office never claimed — is rule and teaching over the congregation: “But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence” (1Ti 2:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prioress as a female superior of a convent of nuns; prior as the superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot; and priory as a convent of which a prior is the superior.
webster_full: PRIORESS, n. A female superior of a convent of nuns.
PRIOR, n. The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.
PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey.
SUPERIOR, n. One who is more advanced in rank or office; the chief of a monastery or convent.
GUIDE, v.t. To lead or direct in a way; to conduct; also, to regulate and manage; to direct the affairs of.
scriptures: I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully.
Tit 2:3
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.
corruption_summary: The superior of a house of nuns: genuine household authority of a kind Scripture honours, inside a system that offered a devout woman a wall instead of a home.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour Scripture already places on a woman's oversight of a household. “She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness” (Pro 31:27) describes real administration, and the churches that treat a wife and mother as managing nothing have not read it.

The live corruption is the system around the office rather than the office itself: a church that ranked the veil above the home pushed its ablest daughters toward a priory because it had no higher word for a household. Scripture needs no higher word, since it has already given the household the commands — “I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house” (1Ti 5:14).
roots_summary: Latin prior, former or superior; Greek oikodespotes (G3617), master of a house; Greek presbutis (G4247), an aged woman; Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength or worth; Greek kalodidaskalos (G2567), a teacher of good things.
roots_lines: Latin prior — former, first, superior; a comparative, so the title itself implies someone above her.
Greek presbutis (G4247) — an aged woman; “teachers of good things” (Tit 2:3).
Greek kalodidaskalos (G2567) — a teacher of what is good; the office Paul gives older women.
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, ability, worth; the virtuous woman's own word.
Greek oikodespotes (G3617) — master of a household; the sphere of a prioress's real authority.
usage: “She looketh well to the ways of her household” (Pro 31:27) — administration Scripture commends in a woman.
“in behaviour as becometh holiness” (Tit 2:3) — the character of an older woman in charge.
“nor to usurp authority over the man” (1Ti 2:12) — the boundary the office did not cross.

pos: n. (the monk charged with training novices through their probationary year and judging their fitness to profess)
etymology: Latin novicius, new, from novus, new; with magister, a master or teacher. The teacher of the new.
biblical_def: The novice master trained the novices: he taught them the rule, the psalter and the ceremonies, tested their temper and their motives, and reported whether each should be allowed to profess. The office presumes something sound — that a man should be proved before he is admitted to responsibility — and Scripture presumes the same. “And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless” (1Ti 3:10); “Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1Ti 3:6) uses the very word. Spiritual immaturity is a real category and is to be fed accordingly: “As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2), and “I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it” (1Co 3:2). So a church with no notion of probation, which puts a new convert on a platform, has abandoned a plain apostolic rule. The monastic application went wrong only in what it was proving a man for: the end of the training was an irrevocable vow rather than a settled Christian life, and a year is short measure for a lifetime.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines novice as one who is new in any business, a beginner, and one newly received into a monastery during probation; novitiate as the state or time of learning rudiments; and probation as trial, examination, proof.
webster_full: NOVICE, n. One who is new in any business; one unacquainted or unskilled; a beginner; also, one newly received into a monastery, during the time of probation.
NOVITIATE, n. The state or time of learning rudiments; in religious houses, a year or other time of probation for the trial of a religious person.
PROBATION, n. The act of proving; proof; trial; also, moral trial; the state of a person in which he has opportunity to prove his character.
MASTER, n. One who teaches; an instructor; a teacher; one uncommonly skilled in any occupation or science.
PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality by experiment; to examine; to test.
scriptures: And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.
Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able.
corruption_summary: The trainer of novices: probation before responsibility is a plain apostolic rule, aimed here at an irrevocable vow a year cannot responsibly prove.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is probation itself. “let these also first be proved” (1Ti 3:10) is directed at ordinary church office and is widely ignored; the cloister at least took it seriously enough to build a year and an officer around it.

The live defect is the object of the training. A novitiate that ends in lifelong vows of poverty, chastity and obedience is proving a young man for an undertaking Scripture never required of him, and “lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1Ti 3:6) warns about exactly the self-confidence such a profession invites. Train men; do not bind them.
roots_summary: Latin novicius, new; Greek neophutos (G3504), newly planted; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test; Greek nepios (G3516), an infant; Greek didasko (G1321), to teach.
roots_lines: Greek neophutos (G3504) — newly planted; “Not a novice” (1Ti 3:6) is this one word.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove by trial; “And let these also first be proved” (1Ti 3:10).
Greek nepios (G3516) — an infant, one without speech; Paul's word for the spiritually immature.
Greek didasko (G1321) — to teach; the novice master's actual work.
Latin magister — a master, teacher; the second half of the title.
usage: “then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless” (1Ti 3:10) — probation then office.
“desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2) — what a novice is actually owed.
“for hitherto ye were not able to bear it” (1Co 3:2) — teaching proportioned to maturity.

pos: n. (the annual assembly of the abbots of an order, legislating for and visiting all its houses)
etymology: Latin capitulum, a little head or chapter, from the chapter of the rule read at the daily meeting; with generalis, pertaining to the whole.
biblical_def: The general chapter was the ruling assembly of an order: the abbots of every house met annually — the Cistercians at Cíteaux each September — to legislate, hear appeals, correct abuses and order visitations. It was one of the real administrative inventions of the Middle Ages, and it solved a problem Benedict had left open, namely how a family of independent houses keeps a common discipline without a monarch. Its method is strikingly close to Scripture's. The church in Acts settled a disputed question by assembling its leaders to deliberate: “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6). Wisdom in a plurality is a standing principle — “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) and “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22). And the end of order is peace: “For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1Co 14:33). A Presbyterian will notice the resemblance to a synod, and he should: the Cistercian chapter is a conciliar answer to a monarchical church, and it worked for as long as it kept meeting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chapter as an assembly of the monks of a convent, or of the prebends of a collegiate church; general as relating to a whole genus or kind, not special or particular; and council as an assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the monks of a convent, or of the prebends of a collegiate or cathedral church.
CHAPTER, n. A division of a book or writing; a section or part of a book.
GENERAL, a. Relating to a whole genus or kind; comprehending many species or individuals; not special or particular.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; also, the object of a visit; and in an official sense, the act of a superior examining into the state of a diocese or church.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
corruption_summary: The annual assembly of an order's abbots: a conciliar answer to a monarchical church, sound in method, and only as good as its attendance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is deliberation among a plurality of accountable leaders. “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) is the pattern, and churches governed by one unaccountable man are further from it than a thirteenth-century Cistercian chapter was.

The live defect is decay by non-attendance. A chapter that legislates annually and is ignored becomes a paper discipline, and by the fifteenth century many abbots simply stopped travelling; the reform orders were born partly because the chapters had lapsed. “There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand” (Pro 19:21) is the proportion — good structures are worth having and none of them is self-sustaining.
roots_summary: Latin capitulum, a chapter; Greek sunedrion, a council; Greek presbuterion (G4244), a body of elders; Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel; Greek sumbouleuo (G4823), to take counsel together.
roots_lines: Latin capitulum — a little head, a chapter; the meeting is named for the chapter of the rule read at it.
Greek presbuterion (G4244) — a body of elders; the New Testament's plural leadership.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).
Greek sumbouleuo (G4823) — to consult together; the action of a chapter or a synod.
Greek taxis (G5010) — order, arrangement; the end “not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33) names.
usage: “came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — the apostolic precedent for an assembly.
“in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22) — the wisdom of a plurality.
“God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33) — the purpose of church order.

pos: n. (the formal inspection of a religious house by its bishop, abbot or order, with power to correct)
etymology: Latin visitatio, a visiting, from visitare, to go to see; the official coming to inspect and correct.
biblical_def: A monastic visitation was a formal inspection: the bishop, or the abbot of the mother house, or a commissary of the general chapter, came to a religious house, examined each member separately, heard complaints, read the accounts and issued injunctions. The surviving records are among the frankest documents of the Middle Ages, cataloguing everything from ruined roofs to drunkenness to abbots who had pawned the plate. Visitation rests on a biblical conviction, that oversight must be exercised and not assumed. “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28) lays the duty on the overseer; and Paul himself practised the thing: “Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do” (Act 15:36). The word itself carries a weightier sense in Scripture, where God's own visitation is either mercy or judgment — “because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” (Luk 19:44). A house that dreaded the bishop's coming was rehearsing something larger, and the frankness of the records is to the system's credit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines visitation as the act of visiting, and in an official sense the act of a superior who visits a diocese, church or college to inspect its state; and inspect as to look on or into, to view and examine.
webster_full: VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; also, the act of a superior or superintending officer, who visits a corporation, college, church or other house, to examine into the manner in which it is conducted.
VISITATION, n. Communication of divine love; also, in a judicial sense, the sending of some affliction or trial.
VISITOR, n. One who visits; also, a superior officer who visits an institution to inspect its state and proceedings.
INSPECT, v.t. To look on or into; to view and examine; to look at or over for the purpose of ascertaining the quality or condition of a thing.
INJUNCTION, n. A command; order; precept; the act of enjoining or directing.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do.
And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
corruption_summary: The formal inspection of a religious house: oversight actually exercised, in records frank enough to have supplied the case against the monasteries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is oversight that inspects. Many congregations have overseers in name whose only information about the flock is what reaches them unasked; Paul's own practice was to go and look — “and see how they do” (Act 15:36).

The live defect of the medieval system was that visitation could be bought off, evaded by exempt houses, or conducted so perfunctorily that the injunctions were copied from the last visit. The limit on the visitor is also scriptural: “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — a man with power to correct must not become a lord, and some visitors plainly did.
roots_summary: Latin visitare, to go and see; Greek episkope (G1984), oversight or visitation; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Hebrew paqad (H6485), to visit or muster; Greek episkeptomai (G1980), to look after.
roots_lines: Greek episkope (G1984) — oversight, and also a visitation; “the time of thy visitation” (Luk 19:44).
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer; “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28).
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, number, appoint; in the prophets usually God coming to reckon.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to go and look after; the verb of visiting the sick and the orphan.
Latin visitatio — a visiting; the administrative term that survives in English church law.
usage: “and see how they do” (Act 15:36) — apostolic visitation, plainly stated.
“Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) — the duty that requires inspection.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the limit on every visitor.

pos: n. (the holding of a benefice or abbey in trust by one who does not serve it, drawing its revenue; the abuse of the commendatory abbot)
etymology: Latin in commendam, in trust or keeping, from commendare, to commit to the care of; a benefice committed to a man's keeping until it should be properly filled.
biblical_def: To hold a house in commendam was to be given its revenues in trust, pending a proper appointment, without being its working head. The device began innocently, as a way to keep a vacant abbey's income safe, and became one of the most destructive abuses in the late medieval church: abbeys were handed to royal favourites, boy cardinals and absentee bishops who drew the rents and never saw the cloister, while the monks lived on a fraction and the buildings decayed. Scripture's treatment of a hireling shepherd fits exactly. “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12); and Ezekiel's indictment of shepherds who feed themselves is the Old Testament form: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). Scripture does provide that those who serve be supported — “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17) — and the words rule well and labour are precisely what a commendatory abbot did not do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commendam as a benefice or living commended to the care of a clerk till a proper pastor is provided, a void benefice held in trust; and hireling as one who is hired, or who serves for wages, with a mercenary sense.
webster_full: COMMENDAM, n. In ecclesiastical law, a benefice or living commended, by the gift of the king or other patron, to the care of a clerk, to hold till a proper pastor is provided.
COMMENDATORY, a. Holding a benefice in commendam; as a commendatory abbot.
HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages; usually in a contemptuous sense, a mercenary.
BENEFICE, n. In the church, an ecclesiastical living, or preferment; a church endowed with a revenue for the maintenance of divine service.
ABSENTEE, n. One who is absent; one who withdraws from his country or from the place where his estate or office requires his presence.
scriptures: But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Jer 23:1
Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: An abbey's revenue drawn by a man who never served it: the hireling shepherd made a system of law, and a principal cause of monastic decay.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is total and Scripture names it without hedging. A man paid by a flock he does not feed is a hireling, and the Lord contrasts him with himself: “whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12). Jeremiah pronounces the sentence: “Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD” (Jer 23:1). That commendam was lawful, customary and papally granted changes nothing about it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that support follows labour. “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour” (1Ti 5:17) makes ruling well the ground of the honour, and any arrangement that pays a title rather than a work — in any church, of any tradition — is commendam in modern dress.
roots_summary: Latin commendare, to commit to another's keeping; Greek misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Hebrew roeh (H7462), a shepherd; Greek poimen (G4166), a shepherd; Greek kopiao (G2872), to labour to weariness.
roots_lines: Latin in commendam — in trust; the legal fiction that a revenue was merely being kept safe.
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired man; “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd” (Joh 10:12).
Hebrew roeh (H7462) — a shepherd, one who feeds; “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2).
Greek poimen (G4166) — a shepherd, pastor; the office commendam emptied.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to toil to weariness; “especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17).
usage: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!” (Eze 34:2) — the prophetic verdict on the arrangement.
“and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12) — the hireling's behaviour when it costs him something.
“Let the elders that rule well” (1Ti 5:17) — support tied to labour, which commendam severed.

pos: n. (the annexing of a parish's tithes to a monastery or layman, leaving a stipendiary vicar to do the work)
etymology: Latin in and proprius, one's own: the making over of a benefice as another's property. Called appropriation when the holder is ecclesiastical, impropriation when lay.
biblical_def: Impropriation is the annexing of a parish's tithes to a religious house or, after the dissolution, to a layman, who then paid a poor vicar to serve the cure. By the eve of the Reformation a large share of English parishes were impropriate, and the consequence was structural: the tithe went to an abbey or a gentleman, while the man who buried the dead and preached on Sunday lived on a stipend. Scripture ties the tithe to the service and to the servant. “I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve” (Num 18:21) — for their service, which is the whole point. Nehemiah treats the diversion of that portion as a scandal requiring reform: “And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them: for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field” (Neh 13:10). Paul applies the principle to the gospel ministry: “Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple?” (1Co 9:13), and “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impropriation as the act of putting an ecclesiastical benefice in the hands of a layman, and the benefice so held; appropriation as the severing of a benefice to the perpetual use of a religious house; and vicar as one who performs the duties of another.
webster_full: IMPROPRIATION, n. The act of putting an ecclesiastical benefice in the hands of a layman; also, a benefice in the hands of a layman.
IMPROPRIATE, v.t. To appropriate to private use; to appropriate, as a benefice, to a layman.
APPROPRIATION, n. In law, the severing of a benefice ecclesiastical from its original use, whereby it becomes the property of some religious house.
VICAR, n. The incumbent of an appropriated or impropriated benefice; one who performs the duties of another; a substitute.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support.
scriptures: And, behold, I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve, even the service of the tabernacle of the congregation.
And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them: for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field.
Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
corruption_summary: A parish's tithes annexed elsewhere while a stipendiary vicar does the work: the portion severed from the service, which Nehemiah treated as a scandal.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is severing the portion from the service, and Nehemiah supplies both the diagnosis and the remedy. He found the Levites had abandoned the temple because they were not being paid — “the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field” (Neh 13:10) — and he reinstated them. Impropriation institutionalised that abuse for centuries, and the perpetual poverty of English vicarages was its direct result.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that giving should reach the people doing the work. “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn” (1Ti 5:18) is Paul's chosen image, and it is deliberately agricultural: the animal that does the threshing eats from the floor it threshes.
roots_summary: Latin proprius, one's own; Hebrew maaser (H4643), a tithe; Hebrew abodah (H5656), service; Greek misthos (G3408), reward or wages; Greek ergates (G2040), a labourer.
roots_lines: Latin proprius — one's own; the word records exactly what happened to the benefice.
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tenth, a tithe; “all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance” (Num 18:21).
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — service, labour; the tithe is given for their service.
Greek ergates (G2040) — a labourer, workman; “The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18).
Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, hire; what the vicar was paid a fraction of.
usage: “the portions of the Levites had not been given them” (Neh 13:10) — the abuse named and corrected.
“they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar” (1Co 9:13) — the portion tied to the service.
“Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me” (Mal 3:8) — the gravity Scripture attaches to a diverted tithe.
